screens.title: What is SSH and how key-based authentication works
screens.narratorSegment: SSH is a cryptographic network protocol used for secure remote access and data communication. At its core, key-based authentication replaces typed passwords with a cryptographic proof of identity. You generate a key pair on your client: a private key you keep secret and a public key you place on the server in the user's ~/. ssh/authorized_keys file. When you initiate a connection, the server issues a cryptographic challenge that only the holder of the corresponding private key can answer. The private key itself never leaves the client; the proof happens through signature exchange. A concrete example: generate an Ed25519 key pair on your laptop, then copy the public key to the server; when you SSH, the server verifies the signature made with your private key and grants access. A common misconception is thinking the public key must be secret—it's safe to share. The dangerous element is an unprotected private key. Always encrypt private keys with a passphrase and set file permissions to be readable only by the owner. Key-based authentication both reduces brute-force exposure and enables strong automation patterns when used with Match blocks and ForceCommand. Reflect: what account behaviors should you change when moving from password to key-only authentication?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Key-based authentication proves identity with a private key; store the public key on the server's authorized_keys.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › SSH Fundamentals
Key concept
Private key stays secret; public key lives in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.
Analogy
Think of the private key as a signed ticket in your wallet and the public key as the verifier's copy. The server checks the signature without ever holding your ticket.
Common misconception
  • Public keys are safe to share; private keys must remain private and encrypted with a passphrase.
  • Key failures are often caused by incorrect permissions—verify 700 for ~/.ssh and 600 for authorized_keys.
Key Takeaway
Keys enable secure, password-less authentication; protect the private key and verify server-side permissions.
Concrete example
> ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "my_laptop_key"
# Follow prompts to add a strong passphrase
# Files created: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

> ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub testuser@remote_host
# Copies the public key and ensures permissions
Check permissions
On the server: chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Incorrect permissions will prevent key auth.
Try this thought
If a private key is unprotected, who besides you can authenticate? Consider the operational trade-off when skipping a passphrase.

screens.title: Generating and protecting SSH key pairs
screens.narratorSegment: Generating keys is a routine but security-sensitive task. Use ssh-keygen to create a key pair and choose an algorithm and key length appropriate to your needs. The chapter shows both an RSA 4096-bit example and the Ed25519 example; for most modern setups Ed25519 is recommended for compact keys and strong security. Run ssh-keygen with a comment to identify the key and always use a passphrase to encrypt the private key on disk. A concrete example is: run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "prod_server_key" and follow prompts to set a passphrase. After creation you will have two files, the private key (for example id_ed25519) and the public key (id_ed25519. pub). Protect the private key with file permissions chmod 600 and, for convenience, load it into ssh-agent using ssh-add so you don't retype a passphrase for every connection. A common misconception is that a key without a passphrase is acceptable for automation; prefer forced-command Match blocks and limited accounts for automation keys, and keep interactive keys passphrase-protected. Closing takeaway: you must balance usability and protection—passphrases plus ssh-agent give both strong security and practical workflow for administrators.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Generate Keys
Command walkthrough
# Example: Generating an Ed25519 key pair
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "prod_server_key"
# Follow prompts, enter a strong passphrase

# Older example (RSA 4096)
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your_email@example.com"

# Protect private key
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
Note: choose Ed25519 for modern systems. Always add a passphrase to encrypt the private key on disk. If you need automation without passphrases, use restricted accounts with Match blocks instead of leaving keys unprotected.
Using ssh-agent
Load keys into memory for the session so you avoid repeated passphrase prompts while keeping your private key encrypted on disk.
# Start agent and add key
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# Then connect normally:
ssh -p 2222 testuser@remote_host
Misconception check: ssh-agent does not remove the need for a passphrase; it merely stores decrypted keys in memory after you enter the passphrase once. If an attacker gains access to your unlocked session, they could use the agent, so lock screens and manage agent lifetimes appropriately.

screens.title: Deploying public keys and permission checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying a public key to a server should be reliable and repeatable. The simplest method is ssh-copy-id, which copies your public key and ensures the target home and. ssh directory exist and have correct permissions. For example run ssh-copy-id username@remote_host or ssh-copy-id -i ~/. ssh/id_ed25519. pub remote_user@host. After copying, verify permissions: on the server, ~/. ssh must be 700 and ~/. ssh/authorized_keys must be 600. Those permissions prevent other users from reading or writing keys and they are a frequent reason key-based auth fails. If a connection still fails, check the sshd logs and run sshd -t to validate syntax in sshd_config. A common troubleshooting flow is: verify public key content in authorized_keys, check ownership (should be the user), correct permissions, and confirm sshd is reading the expected AuthorizedKeysFile path. Remember that ssh-copy-id is convenient, but scripting deployments for many hosts should also ensure proper ownership and SELinux labels where applicable. Closing challenge: if a freshly copied key fails, what three checks will you run first? The correct answers are file contents, ownership, and permissions. Deploying public keys and permission checklist means use ssh-copy-id to install a public key and ensure ~/.ssh is 700 and authorized_keys is 600; check ownership and sshd logs when troubleshooting.. In practical terms, ssh-copy-id, directory and file permissions, and troubleshooting failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use ssh-copy-id to install a public key and ensure ~/.ssh is 700 and authorized_keys is 600; check ownership and sshd logs when troubleshooting.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Deploy Keys
Step-by-step
  1. Run ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@remote_host to copy the public key.
  2. On the server, ensure ~/.ssh is owned by the user and chmod 700 ~/.ssh.
  3. Set chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and confirm the public key line is intact.
  4. If connection fails, inspect /var/log/auth.log or journalctl -u sshd and run sudo sshd -t to test config syntax.
Common pitfall: copying the public key as root or with incorrect ownership will lead to permission errors. Always ensure the file owner is the target user.
Commands & checks
# Copy key
to_remote$ ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub testuser@remote_host

# On server: verify
remote$ ls -ld ~/.ssh
drwx------ 2 testuser testuser 4096 /home/testuser/.ssh
remote$ ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
-rw------- 1 testuser testuser  400 /home/testuser/.ssh/authorized_keys

# Syntax test before restart
sudo sshd -t
Check your firewall and port settings if you cannot reach the server. Misconfigured ports or blocked firewall rules are common when changing SSH ports.

screens.title: sshd_config fundamentals and essential directives
screens.narratorSegment: The SSH daemon configuration file, /etc/ssh/sshd_config, is where you enforce server-side security policy. Several directives are essential for hardening. Set Port to a non-standard value to reduce automated scans. Use PermitRootLogin no to prevent direct root access and require administrators to use a regular account and escalate privileges. Disable PasswordAuthentication no when you want to force keys, and ensure PubkeyAuthentication yes is enabled. AuthorizedKeysFile specifies where public keys are read from; default is. ssh/authorized_keys. To restrict who may connect, use AllowUsers or AllowGroups. Tuning ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax helps detect and disconnect idle sessions. The UseDNS no directive prevents reverse DNS lookups which can slow connections and affect logging. Increase logging detail with LogLevel VERBOSE for troubleshooting. A typical misconception is that changing Port is sufficient to secure SSH; it reduces noise but does not replace disabling weak authentication. Always test with sshd -t after edits and maintain a backup of the original config. Takeaway: decide which directives enforce your security posture, apply them conservatively, and verify connectivity before closing your console. sshd_config fundamentals and essential directives means control access and behavior with port, permitrootlogin, passwordauthentication, pubkeyauthentication, allowusers/groups, and clientalive settings.. In practical terms, key directives to enforce strong server policies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: sshd settings
keyIdea.text: Control access and behavior with Port, PermitRootLogin, PasswordAuthentication, PubkeyAuthentication, AllowUsers/Groups, and ClientAlive settings.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › sshd_config Essentials
Essential directives
  • Port: change default 22 to reduce automated scans.
  • PermitRootLogin no: disallow direct root logins.
  • PasswordAuthentication no: force key-based authentication.
  • PubkeyAuthentication yes: ensure key auth enabled.
  • AllowUsers / AllowGroups: restrict who can connect.
  • ClientAliveInterval / ClientAliveCountMax: detect idle clients.
Misconception: changing Port alone is not a substitute for disabling weak authentication or protecting keys. Port changes reduce noise but do not prevent credential abuse.
Example snippet
# Example sshd_config entries
Port 2222
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys
AllowUsers testuser adminuser
ClientAliveInterval 60
ClientAliveCountMax 3
UseDNS no
LogLevel VERBOSE
Remember to run sudo sshd -t to test before restarting and keep a backup of /etc/ssh/sshd_config when making changes.

screens.title: Hardening workflow and safe deployment
screens.narratorSegment: Hardening sshd_config requires a careful, repeatable workflow to avoid locking yourself out. First, always back up the existing file, for example copy /etc/ssh/sshd_config to /etc/ssh/sshd_config. bak. Edit the file to include your hardened directives. Before restarting the service, run sudo sshd -t to detect syntax errors. If the test passes, open the new port in the firewall before closing your existing session—this prevents losing remote access when changing Port. For example with firewalld run sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=2222/tcp --permanent && sudo firewall-cmd --reload, or with ufw run sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp. Restart sshd with sudo systemctl restart sshd and verify connectivity from a new terminal using ssh -p 2222 user@host. If anything fails, access the machine via a console (KVM or cloud console), restore the backup, and re-evaluate changes. A common misconception is that testing with sshd -t guarantees connectivity; it only checks syntax. Port and firewall configuration, as well as SELinux or TCP wrappers, also affect reachability. Closing question: what steps will you follow locally before restarting sshd to ensure access is preserved? Hardening workflow and safe deployment means backup sshd_config, test with sshd -t, update firewall rules before changing listening ports, and restart sshd with access verification.. In practical terms, backup, test, adjust firewall, and restart sshd safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Hardening Workflow
Step 1: Backup
Create a backup before editing: sudo cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak.
Step 2: Test
Run sudo sshd -t to check for syntax errors. Fix issues before restarting.
Step 3: Firewall
Open the new port before restart. Example: sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=2222/tcp --permanent && sudo firewall-cmd --reload.
Step 4: Restart & verify
Restart: sudo systemctl restart sshd, then verify by connecting from a new session: ssh -p 2222 user@host.

screens.title: SSH agent forwarding and X11 forwarding
screens.narratorSegment: Agent forwarding and X11 forwarding are useful features but carry risk if used without care. Agent forwarding, enabled with ssh -A, allows a remote host to use your local private key for further SSH connections without copying the private key to that host. This is practical for connecting from a bastion host to internal machines, but if the intermediate host is compromised, an attacker may use the forwarded agent to authenticate elsewhere during the session. A safer pattern is to forward only when necessary and avoid agent-forwarding on untrusted hosts. X11 forwarding, enabled with ssh -X, lets graphical applications running on the remote server display locally. It can be convenient for administrative tools but increases the attack surface and may leak data through the X channel. Use X11 forwarding sparingly and prefer secure alternatives like remote browser-based tools if available. A common misconception is that agent forwarding copies your private key—this is false; it proxies authentication via the agent. Closing takeaway: use agent and X11 forwarding only when required and prefer restricted Match blocks and temporary forwarding rather than broad, permanent allowances.

narration.text: Agent forwarding and X11 forwarding are useful features but carry risk if used without care. Agent forwarding, enabled with ssh -A, allows a remote host to use your local private key for further SSH connections without copying the private key to that host. This is practical for connecting from a bastion host to internal machines, but if the intermediate host is compromised, an attacker may use the forwarded agent to authenticate elsewhere during the session. A safer pattern is to forward only when necessary and avoid agent-forwarding on untrusted hosts. X11 forwarding, enabled with ssh -X, lets graphical applications running on the remote server display locally. It can be convenient for administrative tools but increases the attack surface and may leak data through the X channel. Use X11 forwarding sparingly and prefer secure alternatives like remote browser-based tools if available. A common misconception is that agent forwarding copies your private key—this is false; it proxies authentication via the agent. Closing takeaway: use agent and X11 forwarding only when required and prefer restricted Match blocks and temporary forwarding rather than broad, permanent allowances.

keyIdea.title: Forwarding trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Agent and X11 forwarding increase convenience but expand trust boundaries; forward only to trusted hosts and for limited sessions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Forwarding Features
Agent forwarding
Enable with ssh -A user@host. It proxies your local agent so the remote host can ask it to sign requests for other SSH servers. It does not copy the private key, but an attacker on the remote host could use the forwarded agent during the session.
Safe practice
  • Forward only from trusted client machines to trusted hosts.
  • Limit agent lifetime and use SSH sockets with restricted permissions.
X11 forwarding
Enable with ssh -X user@host. It allows remote GUIs to appear locally but increases exposure. Consider alternatives for critical systems.
Misconception check
Agent forwarding does not equal key copying. X11 forwarding does open additional channels that may leak input or windows to the remote host.
Key Takeaway

Use forwarding only when necessary. Prefer temporary agent use and narrow Match blocks for automation instead of broad forwarding permissions.

screens.title: Local and remote port forwarding (tunneling)
screens.narratorSegment: Port forwarding through SSH provides a secure tunnel for connecting to services that are otherwise inaccessible. Local port forwarding, invoked with ssh -L local_port:target_host:target_port user@ssh_server, binds a local port to a remote target via the SSH server. For example, ssh -L 8080:webserver. internal:80 user@ssh_server lets you open http://localhost:8080 locally and reach the internal webserver through the SSH server. This is useful for accessing internal admin panels without exposing them publicly. Remote port forwarding, with ssh -R remote_port:target_host:target_port user@ssh_server, opens a port on the SSH server that tunnels back to your local machine—helpful when you need to expose a local service to a remote network. Example: ssh -R 8080:localhost:80 user@remote_server will make your local web server reachable from remote_server:8080. A misconception is thinking forwarding automatically authenticates services on the target; it only transports TCP connections. Be mindful of PermitOpen and firewall rules on the server; you can limit which ports are permitted and use Match blocks to prevent unrestricted tunneling. Closing question: which forwarding mode would you choose to reach an internal-only webserver from your laptop, and why? Local and remote port forwarding (tunneling) means use ssh -l for local tunnels to remote services and ssh -r to expose a local service on a remote host; control with permitopen and match blocks.. In practical terms, ssh -l and ssh -r to access internal services securely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Port Forwarding
Local forwarding (ssh -L)
Creates a tunnel from your local port to a target host through the SSH server.
# Example: tunnel local 8080 to internal webserver
ssh -L 8080:webserver.internal:80 user@ssh_server
# Then open http://localhost:8080 locally to access the internal site
Use case: access an internal admin interface while keeping it unexposed to the internet.
Remote forwarding (ssh -R)
Opens a port on the SSH server that forwards back to your local machine.
# Example: expose local web server to remote host's port 8080
ssh -R 8080:localhost:80 user@remote_server
# Then on remote_server, http://localhost:8080 reaches your local service
Caution: only use remote forwarding when you trust the remote server and have controlled PermitOpen settings to limit exposure.

screens.title: Match blocks and ForceCommand for restricted accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Match blocks in /etc/ssh/sshd_config give you fine-grained control by applying directives conditionally based on criteria like User, Group, Host, or Address. They are especially useful for automation or restricted accounts. For example a Match block for a deployment user can ForceCommand to run a single script, disable tunneling, and prevent agent/X11 forwarding. The chapter provides a sample block: Match User restricted_user followed by ForceCommand /usr/local/bin/my_restricted_command and several disables such as PermitTunnel no, AllowAgentForwarding no, X11Forwarding no, and PermitOpen none. A concrete application is creating a git_deploy or git_sync account that only accepts pushes and never gives an interactive shell. A common misconception is that Match blocks are processed in any order; they apply dynamically after global options and are triggered by the connection criteria. Always place Match blocks near the end of the file and test carefully. Closing takeaway: use Match blocks to limit lateral movement and to enforce least privilege for automation accounts—what command would you force for a deployment-only user in your environment? Match blocks and ForceCommand for restricted accounts means use match blocks to restrict capabilities for specific users or addresses and combine with forcecommand to enforce single-purpose accounts.. In practical terms, apply per-user or per-address restrictions and force an account to run only a command. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Match usage
keyIdea.text: Use Match blocks to restrict capabilities for specific users or addresses and combine with ForceCommand to enforce single-purpose accounts.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Match Blocks
Example Match block
# Add to /etc/ssh/sshd_config
Match User git_deploy
   ForceCommand /usr/local/bin/git-receive-pack-wrapper
   PermitTunnel no
   AllowAgentForwarding no
   X11Forwarding no
   PermitOpen none
This enforces a single action for git_deploy and disables forwarding, making the account safe for automated operations.
Best practices
  • Place Match blocks near the end of sshd_config so global defaults apply first.
  • Combine ForceCommand with strict key-only auth for automation accounts.
  • Use Address or Host criteria to limit from where accounts may connect.

screens.title: Common SSH risks and practical mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: SSH servers face several recurring threats. Weak passwords allow brute-force compromise if password authentication is enabled. Direct root login grants immediate full control. Unprotected private keys give attackers the same access as the key owner. Default port exposure invites noisy automated scans, and outdated sshd versions may contain vulnerabilities. For each risk there is a practical mitigation from the chapter: disable PasswordAuthentication to remove password risk and enforce key-only access; set PermitRootLogin no to prevent root logins; protect private keys with a strong passphrase and chmod 600; change the listening Port to reduce noisy scans while recognizing this is security through obscurity and not a replacement for strong auth; keep sshd updated and use tools like fail2ban or PAM-based rate limiting to mitigate brute-force attempts. A concrete mitigation flow when you inherit an SSH server is: disable password auth, ensure pubkey auth is working for administrators, set PermitRootLogin no, open the administrative port in the firewall, run sshd -t, and restart sshd. Misconception: changing port alone eliminates risk — it does not remove vulnerabilities in weak authentication or outdated code. Closing reflective question: which two mitigations will you prioritize on a legacy server you inherit and why?

keyIdea.title: Risks & mitigation
keyIdea.text: Mitigate weak passwords by disabling password auth, prevent root login, protect private keys, change ports carefully, and use fail2ban or PAM limits against brute force.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Risks & Mitigations
Risk: Weak passwords
Mitigation: disable PasswordAuthentication and enforce key-based auth; use PAM for strong password policies if needed.
Risk: PermitRootLogin yes
Mitigation: set PermitRootLogin no and require sudo for administrative tasks.
Risk: Exposed private keys
Mitigation: protect keys with passphrases, set chmod 600, and limit key use with Match blocks.
Risk: Default port scans
Mitigation: consider changing Port, but also enforce key-only auth and rate-limiting tools like fail2ban.
Risk: Outdated sshd
Mitigation: keep the system updated and monitor advisories for cv es affecting sshd.
Risk: Brute-force
Mitigation: use pam_faillock, fail2ban, and disable password authentication to reduce brute-force opportunities.

screens.title: Lab scenario: secure a new production server
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario walks you through securing a new production server. Step one: on your local machine generate an Ed25519 key with a strong passphrase using ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "prod_server_key". Step two: ensure the test user exists on the remote server and copy your public key with ssh-copy-id -i ~/. ssh/id_ed25519. pub testuser@remote_server_ip. Verify remote permissions with chmod 700 ~/. ssh and chmod 600 ~/. ssh/authorized_keys. Step three: harden /etc/ssh/sshd_config—change Port to 2222, set PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, PubkeyAuthentication yes, and AllowUsers testuser adminuser. Back up the config, run sudo sshd -t to test, open the firewall for the new port, then restart sshd. Step four: validate from a separate terminal that port 2222 with key auth works, that root login fails, and that a non-allowed user cannot connect. Step five: create git_sync, add the public key to its authorized_keys, create a simple ForceCommand wrapper such as a script that prints a message and exits, then add a Match User git_sync block disabling forwarding and forcing that command. Restart sshd and test that git_sync sees the message and exits. A common mistake is not opening the firewall for the new port before restart—always keep a second session available for recovery. Final reflection: did the tests show the expected allow and deny behaviors?

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Follow a repeatable flow: generate keys, deploy keys with correct permissions, backup and edit sshd_config, test with sshd -t, update firewall, restart, and validate access.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Hands-on Lab
Starter commands
# Step 1: Generate key (local)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "prod_server_key"

# Step 2: Deploy public key
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub testuser@remote_server_ip

# Step 3: Backup and edit sshd_config (remote)
sudo cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak
# Edit: Port 2222, PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, PubkeyAuthentication yes, AllowUsers testuser adminuser
sudo sshd -t
Restricted user example
# Create restricted account and script (remote)
sudo useradd -m git_sync
sudo install -m 755 -o root -g root -d /usr/local/bin
echo '#!/bin/bash' | sudo tee /usr/local/bin/git-shell
echo 'echo "This account is for Git access only. Interactive shell is disabled."' | sudo tee -a /usr/local/bin/git-shell
echo 'exit 1' | sudo tee -a /usr/local/bin/git-shell
sudo vi /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Add at end:
# Match User git_sync
#   ForceCommand /usr/local/bin/git-shell
#   PermitTunnel no
#   AllowAgentForwarding no
#   X11Forwarding no
#   PermitOpen none
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart sshd

fullNarratorScript:
SSH is the standard secure remote access protocol for Linux systems. In this chapter you will learn how key-based authentication replaces passwords with cryptographic key pairs, how to deploy and protect keys, and how to harden the SSH daemon to reduce risk. We’ll step through generating keys, installing public keys on servers, using ssh-agent to manage passphrases, and configuring /etc/ssh/sshd_config directives such as disabling root login, turning off password authentication, and restricting users or groups. You’ll also explore advanced features like agent forwarding, local and remote port forwarding, and X11 forwarding, plus how Match blocks let you apply per-user or per-address rules. Each technique includes a concrete command example and a common-mistake check so you can avoid permission or firewall problems. By the end you’ll be able to secure a production server: generate an Ed25519 key, copy the public key, harden sshd_config, test with sshd -t, and create a restricted account that runs a single forced command. Consider how each setting balances convenience and safety as you proceed.

Over the next sequence you will master the skills required to securely operate SSH in production. First, you will generate and manage SSH key pairs, including protecting private keys with a strong passphrase and using ssh-agent so you can work without re-entering the passphrase for every connection. Second, you will learn how to deploy public keys reliably using ssh-copy-id and how correct filesystem permissions on ~/. ssh and authorized_keys prevent authentication failures. Third, you will edit and harden /etc/ssh/sshd_config to enforce policies such as disabling root login and password authentication, changing the listening port, and enabling pubkey authentication. Finally, you will practice testing configuration changes safely using sshd -t and restarting the service. Each objective is paired with a milestone so you can verify competency by demonstrating these actions on a test server.

Beyond basics, you will implement advanced SSH features and defenses. You will practice agent forwarding and understand when it is safe to pass credentials through an intermediate host. You will create local and remote tunnels to access internal services securely, and use X11 forwarding for graphical applications when required. You will learn to write Match blocks to bind options to users, groups, hosts, or addresses and use ForceCommand to restrict an account to a single action. Finally, you will identify common SSH security risks—weak passwords, direct root login, unprotected private keys, default port exposure, and brute-force attacks—and apply mitigations such as disabling password authentication, protecting keys with chmod 600 and passphrases, using fail2ban or PAM limits, and keeping sshd updated. These skills prepare you to secure a production server while maintaining necessary operational access.

SSH is a cryptographic network protocol used for secure remote access and data communication. At its core, key-based authentication replaces typed passwords with a cryptographic proof of identity. You generate a key pair on your client: a private key you keep secret and a public key you place on the server in the user's ~/. ssh/authorized_keys file. When you initiate a connection, the server issues a cryptographic challenge that only the holder of the corresponding private key can answer. The private key itself never leaves the client; the proof happens through signature exchange. A concrete example: generate an Ed25519 key pair on your laptop, then copy the public key to the server; when you SSH, the server verifies the signature made with your private key and grants access. A common misconception is thinking the public key must be secret—it's safe to share. The dangerous element is an unprotected private key. Always encrypt private keys with a passphrase and set file permissions to be readable only by the owner. Key-based authentication both reduces brute-force exposure and enables strong automation patterns when used with Match blocks and ForceCommand. Reflect: what account behaviors should you change when moving from password to key-only authentication?

Generating keys is a routine but security-sensitive task. Use ssh-keygen to create a key pair and choose an algorithm and key length appropriate to your needs. The chapter shows both an RSA 4096-bit example and the Ed25519 example; for most modern setups Ed25519 is recommended for compact keys and strong security. Run ssh-keygen with a comment to identify the key and always use a passphrase to encrypt the private key on disk. A concrete example is: run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "prod_server_key" and follow prompts to set a passphrase. After creation you will have two files, the private key (for example id_ed25519) and the public key (id_ed25519. pub). Protect the private key with file permissions chmod 600 and, for convenience, load it into ssh-agent using ssh-add so you don't retype a passphrase for every connection. A common misconception is that a key without a passphrase is acceptable for automation; prefer forced-command Match blocks and limited accounts for automation keys, and keep interactive keys passphrase-protected. Closing takeaway: you must balance usability and protection—passphrases plus ssh-agent give both strong security and practical workflow for administrators.

Deploying a public key to a server should be reliable and repeatable. The simplest method is ssh-copy-id, which copies your public key and ensures the target home and. ssh directory exist and have correct permissions. For example run ssh-copy-id username@remote_host or ssh-copy-id -i ~/. ssh/id_ed25519. pub remote_user@host. After copying, verify permissions: on the server, ~/. ssh must be 700 and ~/. ssh/authorized_keys must be 600. Those permissions prevent other users from reading or writing keys and they are a frequent reason key-based auth fails. If a connection still fails, check the sshd logs and run sshd -t to validate syntax in sshd_config. A common troubleshooting flow is: verify public key content in authorized_keys, check ownership (should be the user), correct permissions, and confirm sshd is reading the expected AuthorizedKeysFile path. Remember that ssh-copy-id is convenient, but scripting deployments for many hosts should also ensure proper ownership and SELinux labels where applicable. Closing challenge: if a freshly copied key fails, what three checks will you run first? The correct answers are file contents, ownership, and permissions. Deploying public keys and permission checklist means use ssh-copy-id to install a public key and ensure ~/.ssh is 700 and authorized_keys is 600; check ownership and sshd logs when troubleshooting.. In practical terms, ssh-copy-id, directory and file permissions, and troubleshooting failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The SSH daemon configuration file, /etc/ssh/sshd_config, is where you enforce server-side security policy. Several directives are essential for hardening. Set Port to a non-standard value to reduce automated scans. Use PermitRootLogin no to prevent direct root access and require administrators to use a regular account and escalate privileges. Disable PasswordAuthentication no when you want to force keys, and ensure PubkeyAuthentication yes is enabled. AuthorizedKeysFile specifies where public keys are read from; default is. ssh/authorized_keys. To restrict who may connect, use AllowUsers or AllowGroups. Tuning ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax helps detect and disconnect idle sessions. The UseDNS no directive prevents reverse DNS lookups which can slow connections and affect logging. Increase logging detail with LogLevel VERBOSE for troubleshooting. A typical misconception is that changing Port is sufficient to secure SSH; it reduces noise but does not replace disabling weak authentication. Always test with sshd -t after edits and maintain a backup of the original config. Takeaway: decide which directives enforce your security posture, apply them conservatively, and verify connectivity before closing your console. sshd_config fundamentals and essential directives means control access and behavior with port, permitrootlogin, passwordauthentication, pubkeyauthentication, allowusers/groups, and clientalive settings.. In practical terms, key directives to enforce strong server policies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hardening sshd_config requires a careful, repeatable workflow to avoid locking yourself out. First, always back up the existing file, for example copy /etc/ssh/sshd_config to /etc/ssh/sshd_config. bak. Edit the file to include your hardened directives. Before restarting the service, run sudo sshd -t to detect syntax errors. If the test passes, open the new port in the firewall before closing your existing session—this prevents losing remote access when changing Port. For example with firewalld run sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=2222/tcp --permanent && sudo firewall-cmd --reload, or with ufw run sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp. Restart sshd with sudo systemctl restart sshd and verify connectivity from a new terminal using ssh -p 2222 user@host. If anything fails, access the machine via a console (KVM or cloud console), restore the backup, and re-evaluate changes. A common misconception is that testing with sshd -t guarantees connectivity; it only checks syntax. Port and firewall configuration, as well as SELinux or TCP wrappers, also affect reachability. Closing question: what steps will you follow locally before restarting sshd to ensure access is preserved? Hardening workflow and safe deployment means backup sshd_config, test with sshd -t, update firewall rules before changing listening ports, and restart sshd with access verification.. In practical terms, backup, test, adjust firewall, and restart sshd safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Agent forwarding and X11 forwarding are useful features but carry risk if used without care. Agent forwarding, enabled with ssh -A, allows a remote host to use your local private key for further SSH connections without copying the private key to that host. This is practical for connecting from a bastion host to internal machines, but if the intermediate host is compromised, an attacker may use the forwarded agent to authenticate elsewhere during the session. A safer pattern is to forward only when necessary and avoid agent-forwarding on untrusted hosts. X11 forwarding, enabled with ssh -X, lets graphical applications running on the remote server display locally. It can be convenient for administrative tools but increases the attack surface and may leak data through the X channel. Use X11 forwarding sparingly and prefer secure alternatives like remote browser-based tools if available. A common misconception is that agent forwarding copies your private key—this is false; it proxies authentication via the agent. Closing takeaway: use agent and X11 forwarding only when required and prefer restricted Match blocks and temporary forwarding rather than broad, permanent allowances.

Port forwarding through SSH provides a secure tunnel for connecting to services that are otherwise inaccessible. Local port forwarding, invoked with ssh -L local_port:target_host:target_port user@ssh_server, binds a local port to a remote target via the SSH server. For example, ssh -L 8080:webserver. internal:80 user@ssh_server lets you open http://localhost:8080 locally and reach the internal webserver through the SSH server. This is useful for accessing internal admin panels without exposing them publicly. Remote port forwarding, with ssh -R remote_port:target_host:target_port user@ssh_server, opens a port on the SSH server that tunnels back to your local machine—helpful when you need to expose a local service to a remote network. Example: ssh -R 8080:localhost:80 user@remote_server will make your local web server reachable from remote_server:8080. A misconception is thinking forwarding automatically authenticates services on the target; it only transports TCP connections. Be mindful of PermitOpen and firewall rules on the server; you can limit which ports are permitted and use Match blocks to prevent unrestricted tunneling. Closing question: which forwarding mode would you choose to reach an internal-only webserver from your laptop, and why? Local and remote port forwarding (tunneling) means use ssh -l for local tunnels to remote services and ssh -r to expose a local service on a remote host; control with permitopen and match blocks.. In practical terms, ssh -l and ssh -r to access internal services securely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Match blocks in /etc/ssh/sshd_config give you fine-grained control by applying directives conditionally based on criteria like User, Group, Host, or Address. They are especially useful for automation or restricted accounts. For example a Match block for a deployment user can ForceCommand to run a single script, disable tunneling, and prevent agent/X11 forwarding. The chapter provides a sample block: Match User restricted_user followed by ForceCommand /usr/local/bin/my_restricted_command and several disables such as PermitTunnel no, AllowAgentForwarding no, X11Forwarding no, and PermitOpen none. A concrete application is creating a git_deploy or git_sync account that only accepts pushes and never gives an interactive shell. A common misconception is that Match blocks are processed in any order; they apply dynamically after global options and are triggered by the connection criteria. Always place Match blocks near the end of the file and test carefully. Closing takeaway: use Match blocks to limit lateral movement and to enforce least privilege for automation accounts—what command would you force for a deployment-only user in your environment? Match blocks and ForceCommand for restricted accounts means use match blocks to restrict capabilities for specific users or addresses and combine with forcecommand to enforce single-purpose accounts.. In practical terms, apply per-user or per-address restrictions and force an account to run only a command. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SSH servers face several recurring threats. Weak passwords allow brute-force compromise if password authentication is enabled. Direct root login grants immediate full control. Unprotected private keys give attackers the same access as the key owner. Default port exposure invites noisy automated scans, and outdated sshd versions may contain vulnerabilities. For each risk there is a practical mitigation from the chapter: disable PasswordAuthentication to remove password risk and enforce key-only access; set PermitRootLogin no to prevent root logins; protect private keys with a strong passphrase and chmod 600; change the listening Port to reduce noisy scans while recognizing this is security through obscurity and not a replacement for strong auth; keep sshd updated and use tools like fail2ban or PAM-based rate limiting to mitigate brute-force attempts. A concrete mitigation flow when you inherit an SSH server is: disable password auth, ensure pubkey auth is working for administrators, set PermitRootLogin no, open the administrative port in the firewall, run sshd -t, and restart sshd. Misconception: changing port alone eliminates risk — it does not remove vulnerabilities in weak authentication or outdated code. Closing reflective question: which two mitigations will you prioritize on a legacy server you inherit and why?

This hands-on scenario walks you through securing a new production server. Step one: on your local machine generate an Ed25519 key with a strong passphrase using ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "prod_server_key". Step two: ensure the test user exists on the remote server and copy your public key with ssh-copy-id -i ~/. ssh/id_ed25519. pub testuser@remote_server_ip. Verify remote permissions with chmod 700 ~/. ssh and chmod 600 ~/. ssh/authorized_keys. Step three: harden /etc/ssh/sshd_config—change Port to 2222, set PermitRootLogin no, PasswordAuthentication no, PubkeyAuthentication yes, and AllowUsers testuser adminuser. Back up the config, run sudo sshd -t to test, open the firewall for the new port, then restart sshd. Step four: validate from a separate terminal that port 2222 with key auth works, that root login fails, and that a non-allowed user cannot connect. Step five: create git_sync, add the public key to its authorized_keys, create a simple ForceCommand wrapper such as a script that prints a message and exits, then add a Match User git_sync block disabling forwarding and forcing that command. Restart sshd and test that git_sync sees the message and exits. A common mistake is not opening the firewall for the new port before restart—always keep a second session available for recovery. Final reflection: did the tests show the expected allow and deny behaviors?

These core items summarize the technical vocabulary you must retain. SSH is the cryptographic protocol that secures remote shell access and data transport. SSH key-based authentication replaces passwords with a private and public key pair: keep the private key secret and encrypted with a passphrase; the public key belongs in the server's authorized_keys file. The ssh-keygen and ssh-copy-id utilities are the standard tools for creating key pairs and installing public keys on remote accounts. Master these basics first, because all later hardening and automation depends on reliably generated and deployed keys. A quick check: can you generate an Ed25519 key, add it to a server, and verify the login without a password? If yes, you have accomplished the foundational competency. Key Concepts — Part 1 means ssh = secure remote access; keys replace passwords; ssh-keygen and ssh-copy-id are the deployment tools.. In practical terms, essential ssh terms and tools. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Finish with the configuration and operational concepts to keep systems safe. The sshd_config file controls server policies: change Port, disable PermitRootLogin, disable PasswordAuthentication, require PubkeyAuthentication, and use AllowUsers or AllowGroups to restrict access. Advanced features include agent forwarding which proxies your local key, local and remote port forwarding for tunnels, and X11 forwarding for graphical applications. Use Match blocks and ForceCommand to constrain automation accounts to a single purpose and disable forwarding for those accounts. Finally, mitigate brute-force and other attacks by disabling password auth, protecting private keys with passphrases and file permissions, and using tools like fail2ban or PAM limits. Keep these ideas in mind as mental checks when you edit SSH settings: test syntax, open firewall ports first, and always have a recovery path. What is the single most important check you will run after editing sshd_config? The recommended step is to run sshd -t before restarting.
